newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: MULTINATIONALS HIT LABOUR STRIFE IN AUSTRALIA COAL.
newsitem.headline: MULTINATIONALS HIT LABOUR STRIFE IN AUSTRALIA COAL.

text.p: Major international mining companies involved in the Australian coal industry have run into a troublesome seam of labour unrest just as they are considering getting out of the once-fashionable business.
A strike at U.S. energy giant Atlantic Richfield Co's Curragh coal mine in Queensland is now in its 14th week as the company works on selling its coal assets.
The Curragh strike, which follows industrial action at the mine in April earlier this year, has completely shut down production, an ARCO spokesman told Reuters on Tuesday.
Even so, the Curragh strike is disrupting Australian coal exports less than the recent bitter six-week strike at Rio Tinto Ltd's Hunter Valley No 1 mine, north of Sydney.
Curragh holds contracts to supply international customers, mainly in Asia, but since early this year what production has taken place has been re-oriented to domestic power stations.

The switch, partly a result of geological problems discovered earlier this year which reduced mineable reserves, caused a reduction in scheduled output to 3.5 million tonnes from five million tonnes a year.
About 210 miners' jobs were lost in the process.
This, together with negotiations over a new enterprise agreement, led to the strike.
ARCO is presently supplying overseas customers from stockpiles and from other mines, a spokesman said.
The strike continues with no end in sight.

However, a new strike at Rio Tinto's Hunter Valley pit was averted on Tuesday after unions the Rio Tinto subsidiary Coal and Allied Industries Ltd agreed to follow an Industrial Relations Commission recommendation that negotiations continue for 21 days.
This still does little to enamour international mining giants with Australia's low-return strike-prone coal industry.
An ARCO spokesman told Reuters the group continued to review options with its Australian coal assets.

A decision would be taken toward the end of the year on whether the assets would be sold to the trade or floated off through a share issue, he said. An information memorandum on market value would be released soon, he added.
Potential buyers had shown interest for months, although formal offers were not yet on the table, he said.
The ongoing strike was not seen as detrimental to the sale, with valuation of assets and selloff decisions to be based on long-term values and strategic considerations, he said.
When Curragh was first hit by strikes earlier this year, ARCO said production was being lost at the rate of 100,000 tonnes of thermal and coking coal a week.
Coal and Allied's Hunter Valley No 1 mine normally produces more, at about 25,000 tonnes of semi-soft coking coal and thermal coal a day, for export to Japan elsewhere in east Asia.
But the mine contributed greatly to the net loss of A$8.76 million which the company incurred in the six months to June.
Exxon Corp also has its New South Wales coal mining assets up for sale.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
